name: Nurikabe
description: A Japanese yōkai of folklore from northern Kyushu that manifests as an invisible barrier blocking the path of nighttime travelers. Defeating it traditionally requires sweeping a stick along its base.
full_description: Nurikabe (塗壁, ぬりかべ, 'plastered wall') is a yōkai documented in folk traditions of northern Kyushu — particularly Onga County in former Chikuzen Province (modern Fukuoka Prefecture) and adjacent parts of Ōita Prefecture. It manifests as an invisible obstruction that suddenly bars a traveler's path on a road at night: attempts to walk around or above it fail, since the wall extends as needed. Folklorist Kunio Yanagita's 1938 collection records that 'when one is walking a path at night, suddenly the destination one is going towards turns into a wall'. The traditional remedy, recorded in the same regional sources, is to sweep a stick along the bottom of the wall — striking the top has no effect. Until 2007 the creature was thought to lack any pre-modern visual representation; that year, a c. 1660 yōkai handscroll held by Brigham Young University was identified as containing a labelled illustration of nurikabe shown as a three-eyed, dog-elephant-like beast, which is now considered the earliest extant depiction. The modern, beloved visual identity of nurikabe — a great rectangular wall with arms, legs and a face — was created by manga artist Mizuki Shigeru, who said the design grew out of a personal experience of an invisible obstruction during the Pacific War in New Guinea. Through Mizuki's GeGeGe no Kitarō series the character became a national icon. Skeptics and some cultural commentators interpret the original folk experience as a sleep-deprivation, fog or ground-hugging mist phenomenon known to nighttime travelers in the Kyushu countryside.

aliases.name: Nurikabe
aliases.meaning: From nuru ('to plaster, paint') + kabe ('wall'); 'plastered wall'

origin: Indigenous folk tradition is concentrated in northern Kyushu, especially Fukuoka Prefecture (former Chikuzen Province) and Ōita Prefecture. The figure is now nationally and internationally recognised through Mizuki Shigeru's manga.

etymology.origin: Japanese: 塗 (nuru, 'to plaster, paint, smear') + 壁 (kabe, 'wall')
etymology.meaning: 'Plastered wall' or 'painted wall'; also rendered 塗り壁
etymology.first_use: Recorded in 20th-century Kyushu folklore collections (notably Yanagita Kunio, 1938); the BYU c. 1660 scroll labels its creature 'nurikabe', placing the term in the mid-Edo period

timeline.event: Earliest known illustrated record: a yōkai handscroll labelled with the name 'nurikabe', later acquired by the L. Tom Perry Special Collections at Brigham Young University
timeline.significance: Pushes documented existence of the figure to the mid-Edo period

timeline.event: Folklorist Kunio Yanagita publishes accounts of nurikabe in folk-tale collections, locating it in Onga County, Fukuoka
Mizuki Shigeru's GeGeGe no Kitarō introduces the iconic anthropomorphic wall design
timeline.significance: Modern visual identity of nurikabe; the character becomes a member of Kitarō's troupe

timeline.event: Yumoto Kōichi identifies the c. 1660 BYU scroll's creature as a labelled nurikabe
timeline.significance: First confirmed pre-modern image of the yōkai

related.name: Nobiagari
related.description: Yōkai that grows taller and taller before a traveler, similarly obstructive

related.name: Betobeto-san
related.description: Invisible road yōkai that follows night travelers

related.name: Tanuki
related.description: In some regional accounts, mischievous tanuki are blamed for the same disorienting nighttime experiences

related.name: Nurarihyon
related.description: Similarly known mainly through Edo emaki and revived by Mizuki Shigeru

cultural_notes: Tradition interprets nighttime obstruction on lonely roads as a yōkai attack rather than mere disorientation; the stick-sweeping remedy is canonical.
